claims.claim: David Mitchell states that Earthsea’s accents and dialects are mentioned in the narration but never written out phonetically on the page.
claims.source: David Mitchell, "David Mitchell on Earthsea: a rival to Tolkien and George RR Martin", The Guardian, 23 October 2015
claims.quote: accents and dialects are referred to but not reproduced on

claims.claim: David Mitchell states that the dialogue of A Wizard of Earthsea carries warmth and humour but contains no knowing wisecracks.
claims.source: David Mitchell, "David Mitchell on Earthsea: a rival to Tolkien and George RR Martin", The Guardian, 23 October 2015
claims.quote: Dialogue contains warmth and humour, but no knowing wisecracks

claims.claim: Margaret Atwood characterises the closing scene of The Birthday of the World as a minimalist dance and quotes it as the book’s last words.
claims.source: Margaret Atwood, "The Queen of Quinkdom", The New York Review of Books, 26 September 2002 issue
claims.quote: ends with a minimalist dance, as an old woman

claims.feature: other: process over theory in forewords
claims.claim: Margaret Atwood states that in the foreword to The Birthday of the World Le Guin describes process rather than theory, giving the genesis of each story.
claims.source: Margaret Atwood, "The Queen of Quinkdom", The New York Review of Books, 26 September 2002 issue
claims.quote: Le Guin describes process rather than theory

claims.claim: The unsigned Kirkus review of Tehanu records that the action moves slowly while Le Guin explores her themes.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of Tehanu, 1 February 1990
claims.quote: the action moves slowly as Le Guin explores her themes

claims.claim: The unsigned Kirkus review of Tehanu says the novel’s philosophy is expressed in thoughtful, potent metaphor.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of Tehanu, 1 February 1990
claims.quote: the philosophy expressed in thoughtful, potent metaphor

claims.claim: Jo Walton calls Tehanu a restless book with very strange pacing.
claims.source: Jo Walton, "A Woman on Gont: Ursula K. Le Guin’s Tehanu", Tor.com/Reactor, 25 October 2011
claims.quote: This is a restless book with very strange pacing

claims.claim: Jo Walton states that she did not believe in Tenar’s life as a farmwife on Gont and that something about it rings false.
claims.source: Jo Walton, "A Woman on Gont: Ursula K. Le Guin’s Tehanu", Tor.com/Reactor, 25 October 2011

claims.claim: Jo Walton observes that A Wizard of Earthsea calls Ged a "young wizard" at its close while The Tombs of Atuan describes Tenar at its close as "like a child coming home".
claims.source: Jo Walton, "Let her be eaten: Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Tombs of Atuan", Tor.com/Reactor, 2011

claims.claim: Julie Phillips reports that after 1974 some readers found The Left Hand of Darkness too oblique and metaphorical and its play evasive rather than illuminating.
claims.source: Julie Phillips, "The Fantastic Ursula K. Le Guin", The New Yorker, 17 October 2016
claims.quote: seemed to some readers too oblique and metaphorical
claims.page: section on the years after The Dispossessed

claims.claim: Richard D. Erlich states that Le Guin’s method in Always Coming Home is a fairly exhaustive ethnography that works by having many voices speak the world of the Kesh.
claims.source: Richard D. Erlich, Coyote’s Song: The Teaching Stories of Ursula K. Le Guin (SFRA digital book, 2009 revision), chapter "Always Coming Home: Future Ethnography"
claims.quote: exhaustive ethnography: having all those voices speaking the world

claims.claim: Richard D. Erlich notes that Le Guin sets a conclusion-drawing sentence in Tehanu off in a paragraph of its own with no transition and no explanation of the phrase it turns on.
claims.source: Richard D. Erlich, Coyote’s Song: The Teaching Stories of Ursula K. Le Guin (SFRA digital book, 2009 revision), chapter "Earthsea Revisited: Tehanu"
claims.quote: marked by no transition but set off in a paragraph

claims.claim: Michael Dirda reports that some critics feel Le Guin’s recent writing has grown windy and soft, too feminist, too mythic, too preachy.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, "The Twilight of an Age of Magic" (review of Tehanu), The Washington Post, 25 February 1990
claims.quote: Le Guin’s writing has grown windy and soft, too feminist

claims.claim: Harold Bloom, quoted in the New York Times obituary, called Le Guin a superbly imaginative creator and major stylist who raised fantasy into high literature.
claims.source: Harold Bloom, quoted by Gerald Jonas, The New York Times obituary, 23 January 2018
claims.quote: a superbly imaginative creator and major stylist

claims.claim: Sylvia Kelso states that where a playwright can score dialogue with silences a prose writer must rely on business, and that in the Tenar and Moss scene the splitting of rushes performs that function.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, "Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin", Paradoxa 21 (2009), pp. 7-22
claims.quote: Where playwrights can score dialogue with significant silences
